newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian opposition say immigration out of control.
newsitem.headline: Italian opposition say immigration out of control.

text.p: Italian opposition parties on Wednesday blasted the government's border control policies and demanded a crackdown on illegal immigration following a spate of violent incidents involving foreigners.

The separatist Northern League party said people entering Italy without proper permits should be sent to work camps while the hard right National Alliance party urged swift repatriation for all illegal entrants.
Immigration hit the top of the political agenda following running battles earlier this week between rival North African drug clans in the usually sedate northern city of Padua.
Recent sex attacks at the Adriatic resort of Rimini allegedly involving Africans and the growing problem of Albanian drug and prostitution rackets have added to the tension.

"You get the impression by looking at what's happened this summer that the government has already lost control of the country," Publio Fiori, a senior politician with the National Alliance, told reporters.
Italy has among the most lax immigration laws in the West and has proved a magnet for African, Albanian and Asian workers seeking a backdoor entry to the wealthy European Union.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Wednesday that his government had already presented a bill which would toughen up immigration control and added it was now up to parliament to ratify the package.
"As far as rules on immigration are concerned, our actions will be completely in line with our European obligations," Prodi told reporters.
Police in Padua said they had arrested 42 people, mainly Moroccans and Tunisians, after two successive nights of bloody clashes earlier this week.
Meanwhile authorities in Rimini have put floodlights on the beaches following two separate night-time attacks on female tourists this week allegedly involving Moroccan immigrants.

"The episodes this summer of rape and violence, especially in Rimini and Padua, show how this most grey and inefficient government has lowered its guard, opening the doors to urban warfare," Franco Franchi, a member of the influential magistrates' governing body, said in a statement.

Italy has grown increasingly anxious about the issue of immigration after more than 16,000 Albanian refugees poured into the country earlier this year to escape an armed uprising in their home country.
Most of the immigrants, who arrived on a flotilla of rusty old boats, have been given temporary visas.
Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano said the immigration law, presented to parliament in February, would help ease the situation. In the meantime he urged calm.
"One has to guard against knee-jerk reactions and irresponsible speculation that associates criminal acts with immigrants," he said in an interview with La Stampa newspaper.
But Mario Borghezio, a spokesman for the Northern League party, said emergency measures had to be taken immediately.

"The security forces know perfectly well where the illegal immigrants are hiding. It is therefore necessary to give them the power to go and arrest them and put them in holding camps or work camps," he told reporters.
